# NFR Machines: Real Limitations on Proprioception and Joint Loading, but Not Actually Safer Than Free Weights

**What it is** — Non-functional resistance (NFR) machines can play a useful supplementary
role but generally cannot match free weights and FR machines for multi-dimensional,
full-range neuromuscular and musculoskeletal training. Many NFR machines force the user to
sit or lie, minimising training effect on major stabilising muscles and involving fewer
joints through fewer degrees of freedom; while potentially valuable early in rehabilitation,
this is an incomplete way of training the body for functional development, since machines
that stabilise major body regions and limit the number of moving joints diminish the
capacity to train balance, coordination and proprioception. The authors give a worked
example: a free-standing squat involves three joints (hip, knee, ankle), while a seated knee
extension machine constrains the body to one joint (knee) to exercise the quadriceps, so for
a comparable exercise intensity over the same range of motion, the machine increases
shearing force across the knee; the squat additionally exercises the thigh adductors, spinal
erectors and other stabilisers, and enhances balance and (via longitudinal compressive
loading) bone density. Seated exercise also always imposes a greater lumbar-disc load than
equivalent standing exercise: maintaining a neutral spinal curve while seated raises lumbar
disc pressure by about 40% (Chaffin & Andersson, 1984); allowing the back to flex forward can
raise this by as much as 90%; a well-designed lumbar-supporting backrest lowers the stress
but lumbar disc pressure can still run about 75% higher than standing; stress increases
further against resistance, especially with jerky movements, and seated positions cannot
absorb shock loading via knee/hip/ankle flexion the way standing can. On safety
specifically, the authors reject the common claim that NFR machines are much safer than free
weights, citing no source for the comparison: injuries to the back and knees (leg press, hack-squat, hip-sled), shoulders and
chest (bench press, pec-deck), elbow (bicep curl machines) and back (back-extension
machines) are "just as common with machines as with free weights," and many machines (pec
deck, bench press, leg press, calf raise, seated press) force the movement to start from the

######

# Breath-Holding (Valsalva) Stabilises the Spine Under Heavy Load; Exhaling Through Effort Is the Authors' Named Risk, Except for Cardiac or Hypertensive Athletes

**What it is** — The authors state that breathing pattern, duration, and rate have a
profound effect on strength production. The Valsalva manoeuvre, breath-holding, plays a
vital role in raising intra-abdominal pressure to support and stabilise the lumbar spine
during heavy lifting, with the abdominal and oblique muscles acting as an anatomical
corset. Spinal stress is diminished during high-resistance-loaded movement against
resistance when breath is held, and exhalation during lifting increases the risk of lumbar
injury; the authors call it unwise to follow the popular medical advice to exhale during
effort during strenuous lifting, squatting, or overhead pressing, though they name that
advice as appropriate specifically for patients with cardiac disease or hypertension.
Common sporting actions, jumping, throwing, pushing against an opponent, striking a ball,
standing up from a squat, kicking, elicit involuntary breath-holding because it enhances
performance and control accuracy in short-duration movements; archery and pistol shooting
stability and accuracy are tied to brief breath-holding phases; other cited research found
speed-strength actions are optimally enhanced when lung air volume is held at about 75% of
maximum capacity (Vorobyev, 1978). The spinal-stress and exhalation-injury-risk claim above

# Continuous Circuit Training Does Not Simultaneously Build Strength and Endurance; Interval Circuit Training Is a Better Fit
**What it is** — Research does not support the claim (made by some instructors and machine manufacturers) that continuous circuit training (CCT) simultaneously develops cardiovascular endurance and strength. Interval circuit training (ICT: high-intensity loading with regular rest intervals) is described as more suitable for developing strength and strength-endurance together. Supporting evidence cited: prolonged low-intensity endurance training performed alongside strength training in the same phase seriously compromises strength/power development, partly because fast-twitch fibres can start behaving like slow-twitch fibres under prolonged low-intensity load; muscle biopsy studies of distance runners' gastr

######## claim--spinal-ligaments-share-load-with-erector-spinae-in-heavy-pulls.md
chapter: "3.7"
# Spinal Ligaments Share Load With the Erector Spinae During Heavy Pulls From the Ground
**What it is** — The authors state spinal ligament involvement during deadlifting or cleans is "invaluable" for reducing the stress placed on the erector spinae, and that spinal flexion during heavy lifts from the ground can damage intervertebral discs; a competent lifter actively increases erector spinae tension to diminish flattening of the lumbar spine during the lift. If this active tension is overdone, the spinal ligaments become slack and most of the load is instead borne by the muscles; conversely, if the muscles are inadequately contracted, excessive stress is placed on the ligaments. The authors describe a skilled lifter as one able to optimize the balance between spinal muscles and ligaments, enha

######## principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle.md
chapter: "8.2"
# Physical Training Must Prepare Tendons, Ligaments and Bone as Well as Muscle, With Heavy or Rapid Loads Playing a Valuable Role
**What it is** — Under "Training of the Soft Tissues" the authors write: "So far, only muscle training has been discussed. However, all movements, especially those executed at high speed, depend on the storage and release of elastic energy from the tendons. Moreover, passive stability, flexibility and protection of the joints depends on the integrity of the ligaments and other connective tissues around the joint." Hence "*physical training must prepare muscles, tendons, ligaments and other connective tissues, as well as the bones*, to meet the demands imposed by the given sport" (PDF 439 / p.428, checked against the page image).  **Why it works** — The authors state: "Research has revealed that the developm

######## framework--kinaesthetic-system-and-feedforward-visualization.md
chapter: "1.14"
# Skilled Movement Depends on the Kinaesthetic System, and Is Shaped by Mental Rehearsal Before It Starts
**What it is** — Skilled movement relies on the kinaesthetic sense, built from four subsystems: joint receptors (joint angle and rate of change), muscle spindles (muscle length and tension), the Golgi tendon apparatus (tension monitoring, protects against excessive loading by reducing tension past a critical value), and the vestibular apparatus (head/body position, velocity, acceleration), plus touch and pain receptors. Proprioception is described as second only to pain in producing the most intense and widespread brain electrical activity. ######## heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol.md
chapter: "4.2.4"
# Loadless Training: Tensing Muscles Maximally Against an Unloaded Broomstick to Train Without Equipment
**What it is** — "Loadless training" (the Russian term; bodybuilders' "posing" training is the related practice) has an athlete voluntarily tense agonists and antagonists maximally without an external load, as if overcoming a maximal weight. In the early 1900s Anokhin and Froshek proposed developing strength through motivated tensing of agonists and antagonists at every joint, as bodybuilders do when tensing before judges, but the technique was not studied scientifically until after 1965. **What it is** — Four trunk claims from 7.4.2 (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418, checked against the page image): (1) the erector spinae "Acting unilaterally ... serve to laterally extend the trunk, whereas acting bilaterally and symmetrically, they extend the trunk backwards without any lateral movement occurring"; (2) "lateral action of the long muscles of the back does not produce spinal rotation and ... the only muscle of the back which is involved in spinal rotation is multifidus. # Restoration Means Help When Organised With the Load, but Routine Artificial Restoration Can Blunt Adaptation
**What it is** — The authors give GPP means a restorative role, important "in those sports in which there are few supplementary training means and training is inherently monotonous ... (gymnastics, weightlifting and cyclic sports)" (PDF p. 368 / printed p. 357, checked against the page image). Two reported gains: with "the sole and systematic use of swimming restoration procedures during the execution of voluminous loading," absolute strength rose 24.2% and strength-endurance 18.9%, against 7.7% and 4.9% in swimmers without them, while training volume rose "by an average of 15%" (Kuchnyev 1977; Platonov 1980); and in highly qualified middle-distance runners before competition, "low frequency vibromassage an

**What it is** — The authors report the Russian dosing rule: "With prolonged use of any given means of restoration, the recuperative effect decreases, so that Russian experts usually recommend that the same restorative means should not be applied more than once or twice a week in the same form. In particular, the body adapts more rapidly to local-effect restorative means than to general restorative means (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). **What it is** — The authors: "Certainly, many of these techniques may work because they are placebos, because the user believes in them. Yet, this is a very good reason not to dismiss them." chapter: "3.3.4.3"

"""Mechanical pre-promotion lint for Flint staged library folders.

Usage: python scripts/lint_library.py <book-folder> [<book-folder> ...]
Checks: body em dashes (header separators allowed), unresolved [[links]] (against staging
library + vault), review-history narration, confidence values, required sections.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from vault_path import vault_library

STAGING = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "staging" / "library"
VAULT = vault_library()
HEADER = re.compile(r"^\*\*[^*]+\*\* —")
HISTORY = re.compile(r"prior version|earlier draft|NO-GO|round[- ]1|round[- ]2|fix pass|fixer|this revision|previous version", re.I)
CONF = {"proven", "supported", "untested", "contested"}
SECTIONS = ["**What it is**", "**When NOT to apply**"]

known = set()
for root in (STAGING, VAULT):
    for p in root.rglob("*.md"):
        known.add(p.stem)
        known.add(p.relative_to(root).with_suffix("").as_posix())
        known.add(p.parent.name + "/" + p.stem)

problems = 0
for folder in sys.argv[1:]:
    for f in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.md")):
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        issues = []
        body_dash = [i + 1 for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines())
                     if "—" in HEADER.sub("", line)]
        if body_dash:
            issues.append(f"body em dash lines {body_dash[:8]}")
        for link in re.findall(r"\[\[([^\]|#]+)", text):
            link = link.strip().removesuffix(".md")
            if link not in known and link.split("/")[-1] not in known:
                issues.append(f"unresolved [[{link}]]")
        if not f.name.startswith("_"):
            m = re.search(r"^confidence:\s*(\S+)", text, re.M)
            if not m or m.group(1).strip("\"'") not in CONF:
                issues.append(f"confidence={m.group(1) if m else 'missing'}")
            for s in SECTIONS:
                if s not in text:
                    issues.append(f"missing {s}")
            h = HISTORY.findall(text)
            if h:
                issues.append(f"review-history words {sorted(set(x.lower() for x in h))}")
        if issues:
            problems += len(issues)
            print(f"{f.parent.name}/{f.name}: " + "; ".join(issues))
print(f"TOTAL ISSUES: {problems}")

# A Lifting Belt Does Not Keep the Back Flat; Its Real Value Is a Proprioceptive Cue for Occasional Maximal Attempts

**What it is** — The authors open 8.9.1 with the two camps: belt users claim "it definitely supports the back"; non-users say "their backs are strong enough not to rely on external support," and "Some authorities regard the benefits of the belt to be mainly psychological" (PDF 478 / p.467, checked against the page image). Their answer: the claim that the belt keeps the back flat "is definitely not accurate, because we all see lifters rounding their backs even when they are wearing thick, wide belts. Strong muscles and not strong belts keep your back flat." But "In one sense, however, a belt can assist you in keeping your back flat - not by lending support, but rather by creating an awareness of the direction of curvature of your lower back," through proprioception. "For this reason alone, it is probably a good idea to wear a belt during occasional maximal attempts, although it is not a good idea to rely entirely on a belt without learning how to position your back correctly and tense the right muscles at the right time. Belts per se do not weaken the trunk musculature; it is only if one persists in relying on a tightly worn belt for long periods that this possibility may occur" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is sensory: "its pressure exerted on the skin and muscles below it tells you a lot about the tension in the muscles, the pressure in your abdomen and the straightness of your back" (PDF 478 / p.467). Relaxed back muscles, not the absence of a belt, are what load "the ligaments and intervertebral discs of your back. No amount of belt support is going to solve this problem" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**When to apply** — Occasional maximal attempts, where the belt's pressure gives the lifter feedback on back curvature and abdominal pressure. Later in the chapter the book points back to "The correct use of the weightlifting belt in proprioceptive lifting training or enhancing trunk stability, sometimes in conjunction with strain measuring devices" (PDF 489 / p.478). Eric's review: the baseline's stated operating value is "safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 41). Inference: the authors' order (learn to position the back and tense the right muscles first, belt only as an occasional cue) fits that sequence.

**When NOT to apply** — Not as routine support on every set: the authors' own caution is against relying "on a tightly worn belt for long periods." No study is cited for any belt claim on this page; the evidence offered is the observation that belted lifters still round their backs, so `untested`. The "weakens the trunk" point is stated as a possibility only ("this possibility may occur"), not as a finding. Note the page's own typo: "helps keeps the flat" (PDF 478), where "back" is missing.

**Example** — The authors' observation: lifters "rounding their backs even when they are wearing thick, wide belts" (PDF 478 / p.467), so the belt did not hold the back flat; the muscles have to.

**Related** — [[claim--lifting-belt-restrains-abdominal-pressure-and-supports-the-stomach-more-than-the-back]] (the belt's mechanical role, same subsection), [[heuristic--redesign-the-weightlifting-belt-wider-front-and-side-buckle]], [[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]], [[claim--spinal-ligaments-share-load-with-erector-spinae-in-heavy-pulls]] (relaxed muscles shift load to ligaments), [[heuristic--use-touch-and-kinaesthetic-cues-to-teach-positions-and-detect-tension]] (the belt as one kinaesthetic contact)

# The Belt Is an External Restraint for Abdominal Pressure: It Supports the Stomach More Than the Back

**What it is** — On the contention that a belt supports the back, the authors write: "A belt actually plays a relatively minor role in directly supporting any load that you may hold overhead, other than limiting the tendency to hyperextend the lumbar spine during the lifting. Your muscles do this job by keeping your skeleton in the correct supportive posture and the downward force is exerted through the joints (including ligaments, cartilages and discs) to the platform. The air in your lungs plays a vital role in this process" (PDF 478 / p.467, checked against the page image). After the breath-holding passage they tie it together: "Without a belt, the pressure within the abdomen stimulates activity in certain of the stomach muscles to act as an internal restraint for the pressure. The belt can assist these muscles by acting as an external restraint for the abdominal pressure. In other words, the belt supports the stomach more than the back. Nevertheless, by supporting the trunk while the breath is being held, it indirectly supports the back" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**Why it works** — The chain the authors give: a brief breath-hold (Valsalva) "increases the pressure in your abdomen and supports your lower spine"; abdominal muscles contain that pressure from inside; the belt adds a restraint from outside (PDF 478 / p.467). Inference: on this account the belt's support depends on the breath being held, since it acts through abdominal pressure and not on the spine directly.

**When to apply** — When explaining to a lifter why a belt helps on a heavy standing lift: it braces the abdominal wall against held-breath pressure and limits lumbar hyperextension under an overhead load. Pair it with the breath-holding rule in [[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]].

**When NOT to apply** — Not as a reason to believe the belt carries load "directly": the authors call that role "relatively minor." No pressure or EMG measurements with and without a belt are given on the page, so `untested`. The overhead-load framing is weightlifting-specific; the page does not discuss squats or deadlifts by name. The breath-hold the mechanism depends on carries the page's own limit: "Prolonged breath-holding (of more than a few seconds) causes dramatic increase in blood-pressure ... definitely not advisable for anyone, particularly older folk and those with cardiovascular disease" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**Example** — The authors' picture of an overhead hold: the downward force passes through joints, ligaments, cartilages and discs to the platform, the muscles keep the skeleton in posture, and the belt's only direct job is "limiting the tendency to hyperextend the lumbar spine" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**Related** — [[claim--lifting-belt-cues-back-position-by-proprioception-but-does-not-keep-the-back-flat]], [[heuristic--redesign-the-weightlifting-belt-wider-front-and-side-buckle]], [[claim--rectus-abdominis-barely-contracts-in-lifting-so-train-obliques-with-side-bending-and-twisting]] (which stomach muscles do the internal restraining)

**What it is** — Having argued that the belt works on the abdomen, the authors propose a redesign: "Like the powerlifting belt, the front portion of the modified weightlifting belt should be wider to distribute the abdominal pressure more effectively, but not so wide as to cause discomfort or impede movement of the abdominal and hip regions. At the same time, the buckle should be shifted to the side to allow you to pull the bar close to the body without occurrence of the fairly common problem of striking the belt in front" (PDF 479 / p.468, checked against the page image).

# Rectus Abdominis Barely Contracts During Lifting; the Obliques Do the Work, So Add Side-Bending, Heavy Lifting and Twisting

**What it is** — The authors: "Contrary to common belief, the abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis) do not contract to any significant degree during lifting or pushing. Studies of the electrical activity of the stomach show that it is deeper muscles of the stomach (the internal and external obliques) which are much more active during lifting. The apparent hardening of the 'abdominals' on straining is usually caused by passive bulging of these muscles and their sheaths. The one time when the abdominals contract powerfully in the standing position occurs during explosive expulsion of air from the lungs or during backward extension of the torso. This implies that abdominal exercises should be augmented by side-bending, heavy lifting or twisting activities to strengthen all the different muscle groups that contribute to stomach and torso stability" (PDF 479 / p.468, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is from EMG: if the obliques, not rectus abdominis, are the active trunk muscles under load, exercises that load the obliques (side-bending, twisting) and heavy standing lifts are what train the muscles used. Inference: the "hardening" a lifter feels under strain is pressure pushing the wall out, so it is not evidence that crunch-type work is training the bracing muscles.

**When to apply** — When a trunk programme is built mostly on sit-ups or crunches for an athlete who lifts or pushes: add side-bending, rotational work and heavy standing lifts. When a lifter or coach reads a hard-feeling stomach under load as "abs working."

**When NOT to apply** — The EMG "studies" are not cited on this page, so `untested`. Two exceptions are on the page itself: rectus abdominis does contract powerfully in forceful exhalation and in backward extension of the torso. The point is about lifting and pushing; it does not say rectus abdominis is unimportant for trunk flexion. The 7.4.2 entry adds that the obliques acting bilaterally "augment action by rectus abdominis" in flexion ([[claim--trunk-rotation-is-driven-by-the-obliques-not-the-erector-spinae]]), so the two sections agree that the obliques matter but address different movements.

**Example** — The authors' own exceptions show when rectus abdominis does fire: "during explosive expulsion of air from the lungs or during backward extension of the torso" (PDF 479 / p.468).

**Related** — [[claim--trunk-rotation-is-driven-by-the-obliques-not-the-erector-spinae]] (7.4.2: obliques drive rotation and augment flexion), [[claim--lifting-belt-restrains-abdominal-pressure-and-supports-the-stomach-more-than-the-back]] (the stomach muscles as the internal restraint), [[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]]

# Cushioned Athletic Shoes Have Not Been Shown to Prevent Lower-Limb Injury; Safety Comes From Learning to Move in a Given Shoe

**What it is** — The authors take on the manufacturers' message that "the primary solution to most athletic injuries is the wearing of expensive footwear" (PDF 479 / p.468, checked against the page image). Against it they set: "fewer injuries occur among those who wear thin soled shoes and that current athletic footwear may even be injurious (Robbins et al, 1988)"; "a much lower incidence of running injuries reported in barefoot populations implies that modern running shoes may produce injuries that normally would not occur without their use (Robbins & Hanna, 1987)"; "running shoes seem to be associated with fewer injuries in fitness classes than so-called 'aerobics shoes'"; Nigg (1986) reports that "on firm shock absorbing mats, the difference in heel strike force is minimal between bare feet, thick-soled shoes and thin-soled shoes," and that "the use of any shoe usually increases the tendency of the foot to pronate, particularly if the impact forces are smaller"; "there is no correlation between the amount of shoe cushioning and impact absorption by footwear during locomotion (Robbins et al, 1988; Clarke et al, 1982)"; and "epidemiological studies have failed to provide evidence that expensive modern athletic footwear enhances protection from injury to the lower extremities (Caspersen et al, 1984; Powell et al, 1986)" (PDF 479 / p.468). Their conclusion: "safety of the lower extremity is not simply a consequence of suitable footwear, but of learning how to move the body efficiently while wearing a specific type of shoe" (PDF 479 / p.468).

**Why it works** — Under "Shoe Design" the authors say design rests "almost exclusively on theoretical models which postulate that shock loading and the inability of the human anatomy to adapt to this loading are the primary causes of running injuries," yet the shoes "do not modify the impact forces during locomotion, a fact which casts severe doubt on the cushioning philosophy" (PDF 479 / p.468). The protective mechanism they point to is in the foot, not the shoe (see [[heuristic--do-some-daily-barefoot-locomotion-to-keep-the-plantar-protective-reflex]]).

**When to apply** — When an athlete or parent expects a more expensive or more cushioned shoe to fix shin splints, iliotibial band pain or "peripatellar pain" (the page's list): the authors' view is that movement efficiency in the chosen shoe matters more. When choosing between running shoes and "aerobics shoes" for fitness classes, the page favours running shoes.

**When NOT to apply** — The page cites studies from 1982 to 1988 and gives no numbers, populations or designs, so `untested` here. Inference: footwear research has moved on since these citations; treat this as the book's position at the time, not a current review. The barefoot-population comparison is the authors' "implies," an inference from incidence, not a trial. The authors also say design neglects "toe, ankle, knee and hip movement in three dimensions" and that "Little work has been done" relating injury to bodymass, height, limb length, qualification, fibre type and other factors (PDF 479-480 / pp.468-469), so they do not claim to know what the right shoe is. They do not say any shoe is fine; they end with "Comfortable shoes should be used which are appropriate for the individual and the sport" (PDF 480 / p.469).

**Example** — Nigg's (1986) mat finding as the authors give it: on firm shock-absorbing mats, heel strike force differs very little between bare feet, thick-soled and thin-soled shoes (PDF 479 / p.468).

**Related** — [[heuristic--do-some-daily-barefoot-locomotion-to-keep-the-plantar-protective-reflex]], [[claim--shoes-delay-the-positive-supporting-reaction-and-alter-lower-limb-recruitment]], [[heuristic--weight-room-footwear-firm-low-heel-and-controlled-slide-for-weightlifting]], [[heuristic--plyometric-surface-footwear-and-simple-apparatus]] (5.2.4: soft footwear and surfaces for plyometrics)

# Do Some Barefoot Locomotion Every Day to Keep the Plantar Protective Reflex Sensitive

# Shoes Delay the Positive Supporting Reaction, and Shoe Geometry Can Change How the Leg Muscles Are Recruited

**What it is** — The authors: "Irrespective of how well designed shoes are, they must be used correctly in different movements. In doing so the user must be aware that shoes always reduce the proprioceptive and tactile sensitivity to the surface on which they are being used." Then a second reflex: "Forces exerted on the shoe are delayed in being transmitted through its shock absorbing sole en route to the foot. The reflex positive supporting reaction (see 3.5.3), which normally operates highly efficiently in bare feet to produce strong reflex extension of the legs and stabilisation of the body, is delayed in facilitating rapid cybernetic control and correction of unsafe movements when shoes are worn. In particular, the locus of application of pressure to the surface of the sole of the foot determines the position to which the limb will extend (Guyton, 1984), so that inappropriate geometry of the shoe can significantly alter the pattern of recruitment of the muscles of the lower extremities" (PDF 480 / p.469, checked against the page image; clipped left-margin letters on "through", "normally", "the body", "worn", "position" and "significantly" partly reconstructed).

**Why it works** — Two mechanisms on the page: a soft sole delays the force reaching the foot, so the reflex that extends and stabilises the leg fires later; and because where pressure lands on the sole sets the limb's extension (Guyton, 1984), a shoe that moves that pressure point changes muscle recruitment. Inference: the second point is about shoe shape, so it applies to firm shoes with an unusual geometry as well as to cushioned ones.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's landing or cutting control looks slow or unstable in a very cushioned shoe; when a new shoe with a different heel or sole profile coincides with a change in movement pattern. The authors' general remedy is to choose shoes "appropriate for the individual and the sport" and use them "safely and correctly, if necessary by studying slow motion replays of the action involved" (PDF 480 / p.469).

**When NOT to apply** — No timing data are given for the delay, and only Guyton (1984), a physiology text, is cited, so `untested`. The page does not say how much delay matters for injury. This is the same reflex the book cites in 5.2.4 to argue against very soft plyometric footwear and floors, so it is one argument repeated, not two independent findings.

**Example** — The authors' fitness-class contrast: bare feet on firm high-density mats preserve "proprioceptive efficiency" and avoid the longer heel-to-ankle lever arm a shoe adds (PDF 480 / p.469).

**Related** — [[heuristic--plyometric-surface-footwear-and-simple-apparatus]] (5.2.4: soft footwear delays "the triggering of the positive supportive reaction of the foot"), [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]] (the positive supportive reaction), [[heuristic--do-some-daily-barefoot-locomotion-to-keep-the-plantar-protective-reflex]], [[claim--cushioned-athletic-shoes-have-not-been-shown-to-prevent-lower-limb-injury]]

# Weight-Room Footwear: No Compressible Soles, Mind the Heel Height, and Weightlifting Shoes Must Allow a Controlled Slide

**What it is** — Under "Shoes in the Weights Facility" the authors say "running shoes or any shock-absorbing shoes suitable for the aerobics class are potentially unsafe in the gymnasium. For instance, compression of any part of the sole during squats, cleans, deadlifts, standing presses, good mornings, snatches, pulls and other standing exercises can cause general instability and consequent injury. Moreover, inappropriate height of the heel can shift the centre of gravity of the body forward, thereby increasing stress on the knee joint and altering the optimal patterns of movement for safe, maximal lifts from the ground. These are all major reasons why powerlifters often wear thin heelless shoes much like ballet pumps." And: "Even firm soled shoes may be dangerous for use in Olympic Weightlifting unless they allow a certain degree of controlled foot sliding necessary for correcting minor trajectory errors of the bar, especially during the jerk" (PDF 480 / p.469, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — A compressible sole lets the base move under a heavy standing load, which the authors link to "general instability"; a raised heel moves the centre of gravity forward and loads the knee. Inference: the sliding point is the reverse case, a sole so grippy that the lifter cannot make the small foot adjustments that save a bar slightly off line in the jerk.

**When to apply** — Before heavy standing lifts, check what the athlete is wearing: no running or cross-training shoes with soft soles for squats, cleans, deadlifts, presses or pulls. For pulls from the floor, prefer a thin, flat sole. For Olympic lifters, a firm sole that still lets the foot slide a little on the platform.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a rule against heels in general. Inference: the page warns against an "inappropriate" heel height; it does not discuss the raised-heel weightlifting shoe, whose heel is part of its design for deep catches, so read "inappropriate" as relative to the lift and the lifter. No injury data are given, so `untested`. The authors' closing line keeps it individual: "Comfortable shoes should be used which are appropriate for the individual and the sport" (PDF 480 / p.469).

**Example** — The authors' own: powerlifters' "thin heelless shoes much like ballet pumps" (PDF 480 / p.469), chosen for a stable base and a centre of gravity that stays back over the feet in lifts from the ground.

# Machine Training Safety: A 24-Point Checklist of Hazards and Countermeasures, and Why Machines Need the Same Supervision as Free Weights

**What it is** — Section 8.10 opens: "It is commonly believed that gymnasium machines are intrinsically safer than free weights and require far less skill in using them. This fallacy is one reason why injuries are still regularly sustained by those who rely solely on machines for training." # Machine Training Safety: A 24-Point Checklist of Hazards and Countermeasures, and Why Machines Need the Same Supervision as Free Weights

**What it is** — Section 8.10 opens: "It is commonly believed that gymnasium machines are intrinsically safer than free weights and require far less skill in using them. This fallacy is one reason why injuries are still regularly sustained by those who rely solely on machines for training." Machines "must be operated correctly to ensure safety and effectiveness," which needs "an adequate knowledge of the merits, deficiencies and the principles underlying the design of each machine," and of how a machine exercise differs from its free-weight equivalent in "which muscles act as prime movers and stabilisers at all stages of the exercise, as well as which tendons and ligaments are significantly stressed" (PDF 480 / p.469, checked against the page image). The list that follows has 24 bullets (PDF 481-483 / pp.470-472, counted on the page images). Grouped here by hazard (the grouping is this entry's, the items are the authors'):
- **Forced lumbar flexion or rounding**: seated vertical pressing machines (round the lower back, lean forward, hyperextend the lumbar spine; seated pressing loads the lumbar spine "as much as 90% more" than standing, Chaffin & Andersson, 1984, so these are not "basic exercises for novices"); seated leg press (backrests that "do not match the natural curvatures of the spine"; "Never allow the weight to return so rapidly that the momentum forces the lumbar spine to round"); lying inclined or vertical leg press (thighs to abdomen: "carefully limit the range of knee flexion and perform the movement slowly"); calf-raise machines; seated back extension (start flexed, end in "loaded hyperextension"; use "only a small range").
- **Forced lumbar hyperextension**: prone leg curl, flat or rounded (place "a roll of firm sponge rubber or towelling under your hip joint"), and inclined (stabilise the hips "or rather use a standing leg curl or pulley machine"); standing leg raise (shift forward off the backrest, "crunching form of a gymnastics 'pike'"); seated bent-arm pullover ("restricting your range of movement").
- **Weak or vulnerable start positions**: bench press machines ("start from your weakest biomechanical position with the bar at chest level," no pre-stretch: a partner helps you begin from extended elbows); pec decks (shoulder externally rotated at the start: a partner pulls the grips forward); a general bullet naming seated bench press, seated leg press, bench press machine and Smith machine: "always ask a partner to help you begin in a safer position and to 'spot' you."
- **Shear, torsion or extra joint load**: hack squat ("excessive shearing force on the knee ... a poor, unsafe substitute for the free standing squat"); seated spinal twist ("strictly upright posture and severely limit range and speed"); standing spinal or hip twisting machines ("little more than useless for 'trimming the waist'"); standing hip adduction/abduction (simultaneous spinal rotation or flexion/extension); Smith vertical press (a larger load on "the spine, shoulders and wrists" than standing free-weight presses); hyperextension machines (hamstrings, popliteus and knee capsule; the knee "tends to be hyperextended").
- **Trunk and hip flexors**: abdominal machines with heel, calf or thigh grips (rely more on iliopsoas; but "there is nothing intrinsically 'wrong'" with recruiting it, "what may be most risky is the inappropriate timing"); sit-up boards with ankle or foot grips (see [[heuristic--after-foot-anchored-sit-ups-stretch-the-iliopsoas-under-load]]).
- **System-level bullets**: any machine that requires you to sit; seated pressing loading the lumbar spine "as much as 90% more" than standing (Chaffin & Andersson, 1984); immobilised joints shifting stress (see [[principle--a-machine-that-immobilises-one-joint-shifts-stress-to-adjacent-joints]]); circuits against the clock; poorly designed, maintained or lubricated machines ("report any such machines to the gym supervisor").

The closing rule: the list "should suffice to increase your awareness that machines are not inherently safer than free weights and that all types of resistance training require learning of the appropriate technical skills for efficiency and safety"; the instructor "should never assume that a client does not need to be closely supervised at all times, even when using machines," because "*continuous observation and spotting are just as important for machines as for free weights exercises* if the safety claims of machine manufacturers are to be realised in practice" (PDF 483 / p.472, italics in the original).

**Why it works** — The authors' recurring mechanism is that a machine fixes the path and the body position, so the user cannot use hips, knees and ankles "to absorb shock or redistribute loading," and "The posture of stable neutral pelvic tilt becomes far more difficult to maintain" (PDF 482 / p.471). Where the machine forces an end-range position or a weak start, the countermeasure is range limits, slower speed, or a partner.

**When to apply** — Auditing a facility's machines, writing a machine circuit for general clients or injured athletes, or briefing new staff. Eric's review: the baseline's operating value is "safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 41). Inference: the closing rule extends "teach before load" to machines, which staff often treat as needing no teaching.

**When NOT to apply** — Each bullet is the authors' biomechanical judgment; only the 90% figure carries a citation, so `untested`. The authors say "The above list is by no means complete." The 90% figure here is seated versus standing ("seated pressing or lifting exercises impose larger stresses on the lumbar spine than their standing equivalents (as much as 90% more, Chaffin & Andersson, 1984)", PDF 481 / p.470); the 4.2.7 entry gives the same source's 90% for a seated back allowed to flex forward ([[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]]). Inference: these are two framings of one cited source, and this entry has not checked which is the original's. Machines built since the book may not share these design faults; check the machine in front of you rather than the category. The hyperextension-machine bullet adds a medical limit: "return to the upright posture after inversion can produce postural hypotension and consequent fainting ... Individuals with abnormally low or high blood pressure should avoid the use of such devices" (PDF 482 / p.471).

**Example** — The hack squat bullet in full: it "can impose excessive shearing force on the knee and are a poor, unsafe substitute for the free standing squat: if you use them, you should ensure that a partner helps you start with your knees extended and that you control the movement carefully at all times" (PDF 481 / p.470).

# A Machine That Stops One Joint Moving Usually Raises the Stress on the Joints Next to It

**What it is** — The last bullet of the 8.10 machine list: "It is important to know that, if a machine prevents any joint from moving, then there will usually be an increase in stress on adjacent joints. For instance, the seated leg extension machine tends to immobilise the hip joint, so that greater stress falls on the nearby knee joint. Similarly spinal stress generally increases for all machines which compel you to push against a load in a seated position. Besides changing to equivalent free weights exercises, you could carefully control the speed and transition accelerations throughout such exercises" (PDF 483 / p.472, checked against the page image). A companion bullet: "any machine which requires you to sit prevents you from using your hip, knee and ankle joints to absorb shock or redistribute loading" (PDF 482 / p.471).

**Why it works** — In a free standing movement the load is shared and redistributed across a chain of joints; fix one link and the neighbouring joint takes what it would have shed. The seated-back-extension bullet gives the same reasoning for the spine: "the seated position does not allow the hip and knee joints any freedom to modify the magnitude or direction of loading on the lower back," so it "can impose a greater compressive and transverse loading on lower spinal structures than an equivalent deadlift" (PDF 481 / p.470).

**When to apply** — Before choosing a machine exercise, ask which joints it fixes and which joint sits next to them; that neighbour is where the extra stress goes. Two remedies from the page: switch to the free-weight equivalent, or control speed and "transition accelerations." Useful when an athlete reports knee pain on leg extensions or back pain on seated presses.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors say "usually," not always, and give no measurements, so `untested`. Inference: in rehabilitation, fixing a joint on purpose to protect it or to isolate a weak muscle can be the right call; the principle says where the cost lands, not that the cost is never worth paying. The 4.2.7 entry already gives the leg-extension knee-shear example with its reasoning ([[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]]); this entry is the general rule the 8.10 list states.

**Example** — The authors' own: the seated leg extension "tends to immobilise the hip joint, so that greater stress falls on the nearby knee joint" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**Related** — [[framework--machine-safety-checklist-hazards-and-countermeasures]], [[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]] (4.2.7: seated knee extension and knee shear), [[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]]

# Foot-Anchored Sit-Ups Recruit the Hip Flexors Early: Curl Slowly, and Stretch the Iliopsoas Under Load Afterwards

**What it is** — From the 8.10 machine list: "All sit-up boards with grips for the ankles or feet compel the hip flexor muscles to become involved from the earliest stages of the sit-up and increase spinal stress, unless one deliberately executes the curl-up phase of the trunk before hip flexion is attempted. If used for a specific training purpose, the average person generally should execute this type of sit-up as a very slow upward and downward curl-up. One of the most negative aspects of doing large volumes of these types of sit-up is their tendency to decrease the range of movement of the hip joint, thereby adversely affecting running, walking, jumping, jerking and kicking efficiency, and increasing lumbar spinal stress. If you do limited range sit-ups, afterwards you should always stretch the iliopsoas muscles under resistive loading to maintain mobility of the hip and lower spinal joints. Long, deep lunges with the trunk upright can be very helpful in this regard" (PDF 482 / p.471, checked against the page image; the clipped left-margin letters of "doing", "timing", "All", "earliest", "trunk", "should", "aspects" and "the hip" are partly reconstructed).

**Why it works** — Anchoring the feet lets the hip flexors pull the trunk up before the abdominals have curled it, which the authors link to spinal stress. Repeated short-range hip flexion in volume, in their account, shortens the hip's range, which then costs running, jumping and kicking. Inference: the loaded lunge stretch restores hip extension range in the same muscle the sit-ups shortened.

**When to apply** — Programmes that use anchored sit-ups or sit-up boards in volume, especially for runners, jumpers, kickers and weightlifters (the page names jerking). Cue the curl-up before hip flexion, keep it slow, and finish with long, deep upright lunges.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a ban on hip-flexor work: the bullet just before says "the abdominal and hip flexor muscles are meant to function in an integrated fashion, so there is nothing intrinsically 'wrong' about doing abdominal exercises which also recruit the iliopsoas group; what may be most risky is the inappropriate timing of the involvement of the different muscles in any trunk exercises" (PDF 481-482 / pp.470-471). The range-loss claim has no data on the page, so `untested`. The page does not give a stretch dose.

**Example** — The authors' remedy: "Long, deep lunges with the trunk upright" after limited-range sit-ups (PDF 482 / p.471).

**Related** — [[framework--machine-safety-checklist-hazards-and-countermeasures]], [[claim--trunk-rotation-is-driven-by-the-obliques-not-the-erector-spinae]] (7.4.2: sit-up variants shift work between rectus abdominis, obliques and psoas), [[framework--stretching-matrix-system-reverse-of-contraction-action]]

# Strong Muscles Protect a Joint Only When They Are Contracted in the Right Pattern; a Relaxed Big Muscle Protects Almost Nothing

**What it is** — Section 8.11 opens: "Exercise texts often state that resistance training is valuable because stronger muscles protect the joints from injury. Electromyographic studies of many common activities show that this is a faulty belief, especially as protective reflexes do not operate or do not operate effectively during many movements involving forced flexion near the end range of movement of the joints." Then: "Muscles can protect only if they are adequately contracted in the appropriate pattern to control the imposed load. Yet, many texts on training for contact sports such as rugby and American football still argue that large, strong muscles prevent spinal injuries, in particular. A relaxed massive and powerful muscle is almost as useless as a relaxed small muscle in protecting a joint. When the muscles are relaxed, the ligaments associated with the joint have to prevent displacement, rupture or dislocation" (PDF 483 / p.472, checked against the page image). Their conclusion: "General strength training on its own is inadequate to guarantee improved muscular protection for the body" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**Why it works** — Protection is an act, not a property: the muscle has to be on, in the right pattern, at the moment of loading. If reflexes are slow or absent near end range, size cannot help; the ligaments take the load instead. The factors that decide whether protection happens are in [[framework--factors-that-determine-muscular-protection-of-a-joint]].

**When to apply** — In contact sports, when hypertrophy or maximal strength is sold as neck or spine injury protection. Inference: in American football, add work that trains the timing and pattern of contraction under unexpected or end-range loads (reactive and eccentric work, braced positions) alongside general strength, since the authors say general strength alone does not guarantee protection.

**When NOT to apply** — The EMG studies are not cited on this page, so `untested`. The claim does not say strength is useless for protection; the authors call general strength "inadequate to guarantee" it, and the next paragraph lists eccentric, isometric and connective-tissue strength among the factors that decide it. It is a claim about joints under imposed load, not about performance.

**Example** — The authors' contrast: "A relaxed massive and powerful muscle is almost as useless as a relaxed small muscle in protecting a joint" (PDF 483 / p.472), aimed at contact-sport texts that say large muscles prevent spinal injury.

**Related** — [[framework--factors-that-determine-muscular-protection-of-a-joint]], [[claim--ligaments-carry-more-load-than-muscles-under-joint-traction-basmajian]], [[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]], [[framework--six-fundamental-principles-of-the-injury-process]]

# What Decides Whether Muscles Protect a Joint: Reflexes, Eccentric Qualities, Coordination, Connective Tissue, and the Initial State at Loading

**What it is** — The authors: "Protection by the muscles is a function of the various extensor reflexes and the characteristics of the eccentric strength of the relevant muscles. It depends on many factors including starting strength, how rapidly the muscles are recruited to contract (the quality of reactive ability discussed in Section 5.3.3), the efficiency of coordinated action by appropriate muscle groups, the strength of the eccentric contraction, eccentric endurance, isometric strength and strength endurance after movement ceases, strength-flexibility, the elasticity of the muscle complex and the strength of the connective tissues involved" (PDF 483 / p.472, checked against the page image). A second dimension is timing: "The protective process also depends on the initial state of the major stabilisers and movers involved when the threatening load is imposed on the body. This load may be imposed on a part supported by isometric, concentric or eccentric movement, or even on a part completely at rest. In other words, depending on initial conditions at the moment of loading, adequacy of protection will be determined by isometric strength and endurance, and concentric or eccentric strength, strength-speed and strength-endurance, as well as by overflow or compensatory muscle activity to furnish supplementary support for the major stabilisers and movers" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**Why it works** — Because protection depends on so many qualities and on the state the joint is in when the load arrives, no single quality can be trained to cover it. The authors draw that conclusion: "General strength training on its own is inadequate to guarantee improved muscular protection for the body. The large range of processes implicated in musculoskeletal protection emphasizes the importance of special strength training in the properly-sequenced, multi-faceted manner discussed earlier in this book" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**When to apply** — As a checklist when a programme's stated aim is injury resilience: count which of the listed qualities it trains (starting strength, reactive ability, eccentric strength and endurance, isometric strength after movement stops, strength-flexibility, connective tissue) and in which initial states (moving, holding, at rest). Inference: the "part completely at rest" case argues for some training where load arrives unexpectedly on a relaxed or holding limb, not only on a muscle already braced.

**When NOT to apply** — The list is the authors' synthesis with no study attached, so `untested`. It names qualities, not tests or doses. It is about protection under imposed load and does not rank the factors. "Overflow or compensatory muscle activity" is the same irradiation idea the book uses elsewhere; it is not separately evidenced here.

**Example** — Inference: a defensive back hit while planting (eccentric state) needs eccentric strength and reactive recruitment; the same player hit while standing still needs isometric strength and quick onset. The authors' list covers both through "initial conditions at the moment of loading" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**Related** — [[claim--strong-muscles-protect-joints-only-when-contracted-in-the-right-pattern]], [[claim--ligaments-carry-more-load-than-muscles-under-joint-traction-basmajian]], [[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (overflow), [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]]

# Under Joint Traction, Ligaments Carry More Load Than Is Believed Unless the Muscles Are Consciously Recruited (Basmajian)

**What it is** — The authors: "Basmajian (1978) reports that *ligaments play a much greater part in supporting loads than is generally believed, unless conscious effort is made to recruit the relevant muscles*. In most situations where traction is exerted across a joint, muscles appear to play only a secondary role to ligaments. Thus, deadlifts, toe-touches and 'aerobic' activities involving flexion and rotation of the spine may rely more on the spinal ligaments than the erector spinae in stabilising the spine. Training to increase ligament hypertrophy and strength thus would appear to be just as important as muscle strengthening" (PDF 483 / p.472, checked against the page image; italics in the original). They add: "Basmajian also questions the validity of 'ligamento-muscular protective reflexes', since reflex muscle activity often fails to occur when a limb is loaded. Apparently a great deal still has to be learned about the mechanics of neuromuscular action" (PDF 484 / p.473, checked against the page image; the clipped left-margin letters of "often" and "neuromuscular" are partly reconstructed).

**Why it works** — Under traction (a pull across the joint), passive tissue is already in line with the load, and muscle joins only if recruited. Inference: the qualifier "unless conscious effort is made" is what makes this a coaching point; deliberate bracing changes who carries the load.

**When to apply** — Programming for spinal flexion and rotation exposure (deadlifts, toe-touches, the page's "aerobic" activities): cue deliberate muscle recruitment, and treat connective-tissue conditioning as a training aim in its own right.

**When NOT to apply** — Basmajian (1978) is cited, not described (no method or data on the page), so `untested`. "Training to increase ligament hypertrophy" is the authors' "would appear," a hedge, and the page gives no method for it. Inference: the deadlift line can be misread as "deadlifts are ligament exercises"; the 3.7 entry gives the book's fuller account that a skilled lifter balances muscle and ligament load and that heavy spinal flexion can damage discs ([[claim--spinal-ligaments-share-load-with-erector-spinae-in-heavy-pulls]]). The reflex point is about limbs under load and is stated as a question, not a finding.

**Example** — The authors' own list of activities that "may rely more on the spinal ligaments than the erector spinae": "deadlifts, toe-touches and 'aerobic' activities involving flexion and rotation of the spine" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**Related** — [[claim--spinal-ligaments-share-load-with-erector-spinae-in-heavy-pulls]] (3.7), [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]] (8.2), [[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]], [[claim--strong-muscles-protect-joints-only-when-contracted-in-the-right-pattern]], [[claim--limb-loading-fatigue-is-often-ligament-and-capsule-tension-not-muscle-fatigue]]

# Attitude and Goal-Specific Visualisation Change Strength and Speed; No Prescription Works Unless the Mind Lets the Body Use It

**What it is** — Under "Non-Physical Factors" the authors write that "the central role played by non-physical factors must never be forgotten. Autogenic training, visualisation, hypnosis, biofeedback, motivational techniques and other psychological methods have formed an integral part of Russian and Eastern European training for many years," and that "even the most meticulous prescription of all the training means and methods in this book will not guarantee success unless the mind enables the body to utilise its full potential during training, restoration and competition" (PDF 484 / p.473, checked against the page image; the left margin is clipped, and "At", "visualisation", "integral", "the most" and "unless" are partly reconstructed). Evidence offered: "it has repeatedly been shown that one's attitude during training or competition has a profound effect on physical performance"; "Highly motivated subjects will usually produce superior performances, especially in the presence of spectators"; "*Visualisation techniques which require the athlete to fervently concentrate on accelerating the training load can increase power and speed of movement*"; and "athletes performed loadless weightlifting movements with a broomstick while imagining effort against maximal loads revealed improvements in strength and skill (Kovalik, 1978)" (PDF 484 / p.473, italics in the original). They predict that "highly motivated, mood-linked, goal-specific visualisation (or 'imagineering')" will "become recognised as a vital part of modern training" (PDF 484 / p.473).

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism on this page beyond motivation and concentration. Inference: the "accelerating the training load" wording ties visualisation to intent to move fast, the same target as compensatory acceleration; the broomstick study ties imagined maximal effort to real strength gains without load.

**When to apply** — Add a goal-specific cue to heavy or explosive sets ("drive the bar as fast as you can"), and use imagined maximal effort with an unloaded bar or stick when load is not available or not wanted. The authors point readers to specialised texts, naming "the extensive survey by Murphy and White (1978) of altered states associated with outstanding performances in different sports" (PDF 484 / p.473). Eric's review: "Constraints-led and external-cue coaching are not part of Eric's practice. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q25): 'I don't apply it, as I don't fully understand it. I want to know more.'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 170). Inference: an "accelerate the load" cue is a cue about the bar, so it sits near the external-cue methods Eric names as a learning area, not in his current practice.

**When NOT to apply** — Only Kovalik (1978) is cited, and only by name; "repeatedly been shown" has no references, so `untested`. The authors limit their own claim on the same page: it "does not imply invoking the vague notions of mind-body power which are helping to market hundreds of self-development courses of dubious validity," whose success "has a great deal to do with the placebo effect (or faith factor)" (PDF 484 / p.473). The steroid sentence ("The increase in aggression by anabolic steroids is also regarded as one of the reasons why these drugs can improve performance") is reported as a view, not a recommendation. The authors also note attitude is "a complicating factor when one attempts to compare the research done on different subjects by different scientists under different conditions."

**Example** — Kovalik (1978), as the authors give it: loadless weightlifting movements with a broomstick while imagining maximal loads improved "strength and skill" (PDF 484 / p.473).

**Related** — [[heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol]] (4.2.4: Kovalik's loadless training in detail), [[framework--kinaesthetic-system-and-feedforward-visualization]] (1.14), [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]] (8.1), [[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]], [[heuristic--protect-the-training-mind-set-from-gym-distractions]], [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]]

# Protect the Training Mind-Set: Reading, Mirror-Gazing, Chatting and TV Break the Focus That Separates Elite Athletes From Average Clients

**What it is** — Straight after the visualisation passage the authors write: "The absence of this state during all exercises is a major reason why the average client in the fitness facility does not improve to the same extent as his elite athletic peer. Book-reading, mirror gazing, social chatting, listening to pop music, TV-watching and admiring the opposite sex in the training setting are all activities that disrupt the mind-set necessary for producing optimal results and are important factors to consider if one chooses to exercise in the average fitness centre" (PDF 484 / p.473, checked against the page image; the left margin is clipped, and "does", "listening", "disrupt" and "to exercise" are partly reconstructed).

**Why it works** — "This state" refers back to the "highly motivated, mood-linked, goal-specific visualisation" the authors have just described (PDF 484 / p.473). Inference: the distractions they list pull attention away from the movement and its intent, which is the thing that state supplies.

**When to apply** — Set-up of a team weight room and session rules: limit screens, phones and social chat during work sets, and give each set a specific aim. Worth stating when athletes train in a commercial gym out of season.

**When NOT to apply** — The page gives no data that distraction explains the client-athlete gap; "a major reason" is the authors' view, so `untested`. Inference: elite athletes also differ from fitness clients in selection, coaching and load, so distraction cannot carry the whole gap. Music is on the authors' list ("listening to pop music"); the page does not separate chosen arousing music from background music, so do not read it as a ban on all music.

**Example** — The authors' list of disruptors: "Book-reading, mirror gazing, social chatting, listening to pop music, TV-watching and admiring the opposite sex in the training setting" (PDF 484 / p.473).

**Related** — [[claim--mental-state-and-goal-specific-visualisation-raise-strength-and-speed]], [[heuristic--arousal-optimum-is-individual-so-fit-restoration-to-personality-and-task-complexity]]

# Four Types of Stability (Stable, Unstable, Metastable, Multistable): Fitness Shifts Between States and May Jump Suddenly

**What it is** — Under "Changes of State" the authors argue that "stability, equilibrium, balance and homeostasis" can "cloud the nature of fitness," because "they create the misleading impression of a fixed level or point above and below which the organism is in mortal danger, operating inefficiently or heading towards breakdown." Physiology "refers religiously to measures such as specific lactate thresholds, normal blood pH (acidity), normal blood pressure, exercise heart rate, the alpha brain rhythm (8-13Hz) and normal blood sugar level," yet "there is considerable variation in all of these measures and in the individual manner of variation from person to person and situation to situation" (PDF 486 / p.475, checked against the page image). They define four kinds of equilibrium: *stable*, "the maintenance of a certain state for a prolonged period, which is returned to after anything disturbs the initial stability"; *unstable*, "the lack of maintenance of any state for a sustained period; any disturbance causes the system to shift to another uncontrolled state"; *metastability*, "a state which persists until a disturbance happens to move it to another state of stability"; *multistability*, "a system that can exhibit stability in not one, but a variety of different states" (PDF 486 / p.475). And "long-term stability is a rarity since the body is always correcting physiological processes so that they constantly overshoot and undershoot certain marks, which themselves are drifting back and forth about an imaginary mean level."

**Why it works** — The authors' conclusion: "it is important always to consider the possibility that there may be more than one type of stability during and after training and that changes in state from an expected norm may not necessarily be undesirable or dangerous. We should also not be surprised by sudden changes of state and not the wave-like transitions that have been discussed in detail earlier in this text" (PDF 486 / p.475). Inference: the sentence reads as "not only the wave-like transitions," since the book's earlier chapters rely on wave-like loading; the printed "and not" is taken as a slip. They suggest chaos and catastrophe theory may explain "these spike-like transients in the fitness state," with "the aim being to produce training conditions to make such events more likely."

**When to apply** — When reading monitoring data against a single "normal" value: a shift away from an athlete's usual level may be a move to another stable state, not a warning. When a sudden jump or drop in form does not fit the planned loading curve. Eric's review: "Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 64). Inference: the four stability types give language for both, a multistable preparedness level and readiness that overshoots and undershoots around it.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual frame with no data, so `untested`. It does not say norms are useless; a shift "may not necessarily be undesirable," which leaves room for shifts that are. The long-jump example is the authors' illustration of rare leaps, not evidence for a mechanism.

**Example** — The authors' example of rare sudden leaps: "the long jump records of Bob Beamon and Mike Powell," which "occur a few times in a lifetime" (PDF 486 / p.475).

**Related** — [[claim--non-equilibrium-and-self-organisation-prigogine-as-a-model-for-performance-leaps]], [[framework--butterfly-catastrophe-model-of-exercise-imbalance-injury-fig-8-9]] (8.8: catastrophe theory applied to injury), [[framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state]] (6.11), [[claim--physiological-thresholds-are-ranges-and-athletes-regulate-performance-by-feel]]

# Four Types of Stability (Stable, Unstable, Metastable, Multistable): Fitness Shifts Between States and May Jump Suddenly

**What it is** — Under "Changes of State" the authors argue that "stability, equilibrium, balance and homeostasis" can "cloud the nature of fitness," because "they create the misleading impression of a fixed level or point above and below which the organism is in mortal danger, operating inefficiently or heading towards breakdown." Physiology "refers religiously to measures such as specific lactate thresholds, normal blood pH (acidity), normal blood pressure, exercise heart rate, the alpha brain rhythm (8-13Hz) and normal blood sugar level," yet "there is considerable variation in all of these measures and in the individual manner of variation from person to person and situation to situation" (PDF 486 / p.475, checked against the page image). They define four kinds of equilibrium: *stable*, "the maintenance of a certain state for a prolonged period, which is returned to after anything disturbs the initial stability"; *unstable*, "the lack of maintenance of any state for a sustained period; any disturbance causes the system to shift to another uncontrolled state"; *metastability*, "a state which persists until a disturbance happens to move it to another state of stability"; *multistability*, "a system that can exhibit stability in not one, but a variety of different states" (PDF 486 / p.475). And "long-term stability is a rarity since the body is always correcting physiological processes so that they constantly overshoot and undershoot certain marks, which themselves are drifting back and forth about an imaginary mean level."

**Why it works** — The authors' conclusion: "it is important always to consider the possibility that there may be more than one type of stability during and after training and that changes in state from an expected norm may not necessarily be undesirable or dangerous. We should also not be surprised by sudden changes of state and not the wave-like transitions that have been discussed in detail earlier in this text" (PDF 486 / p.475). Inference: the sentence reads as "not only the wave-like transitions," since the book's earlier chapters rely on wave-like loading; the printed "and not" is taken as a slip. They suggest chaos and catastrophe theory may explain "these spike-like transients in the fitness state," with "the aim being to produce training conditions to make such events more likely."

**When to apply** — When reading monitoring data against a single "normal" value: a shift away from an athlete's usual level may be a move to another stable state, not a warning. When a sudden jump or drop in form does not fit the planned loading curve. Eric's review: "Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 64). Inference: the four stability types give language for both, a multistable preparedness level and readiness that overshoots and undershoots around it.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual frame with no data, so `untested`. It does not say norms are useless; a shift "may not necessarily be undesirable," which leaves room for shifts that are. The long-jump example is the authors' illustration of rare leaps, not evidence for a mechanism.

**Example** — The authors' example of rare sudden leaps: "the long jump records of Bob Beamon and Mike Powell," which "occur a few times in a lifetime" (PDF 486 / p.475).

**Related** — [[claim--non-equilibrium-and-self-organisation-prigogine-as-a-model-for-performance-leaps]], [[framework--butterfly-catastrophe-model-of-exercise-imbalance-injury-fig-8-9]] (8.8: catastrophe theory applied to injury), [[framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state]] (6.11), [[claim--physiological-thresholds-are-ranges-and-athletes-regulate-performance-by-feel]]

# Non-Equilibrium and Self-Organisation (Prigogine) as a Proposed Model for Sudden Leaps in Performance

**What it is** — Under "Lessons from Modern Physics" the authors say "Many problems existing in exercise physiology research are the result of applying linear, all-or-none, simple cause-effect, isolationist methods to biological and psychological systems of exceptional, interconnected complexity," and that "the schism between 'aerobic' and strength training is a direct consequence of the highly polarised preoccupation of exercise physiologists with cardiovascular activity" (PDF 485-486 / pp.474-475, checked against the page images). The book's attention "to individuality, diversity, asymmetry, delayed effects, conjugate sequences and interactivity of processes is intended to minimise reliance on classical determinism," and "Further progress will undoubtedly be stimulated by borrowing non-linear methods from catastrophe theory, chaos theory and fuzzy logic systems to explain sudden beneficial or harmful changes of state in adaptation space (e.g. supercompensation, muscle injury or heart attacks), as discussed elsewhere (Siff, 1981, 1982)" (PDF 486 / p.475). They single out "The work on *non-equilibrium systems* by 1977 Nobel prize-winner, Ilya Prigogine": "non-equilibrium may be a source of impending order (Prigogine & Stengers, 1984)"; fluctuations "can totally disrupt the existing organisation and produce an unpredictable leap to 'chaos' or to a more differentiated, higher level of organisation (known as a dissipative structure, because it requires more energy to sustain this state)"; and, the "most controversial" part, "order can occur spontaneously or by chance through a process of self-organisation" (PDF 486 / p.475).

**Why it works** — The authors' bridge to training: "Investigation into how specific patterns of training or mental states can promote the conditions for enhanced self-organisation may then be of profit in the quest to produce sporting excellence" (PDF 486 / p.475). Inference: the claim is that training is a perturbation of a system far from equilibrium, and that some leaps in fitness may come from reorganisation rather than steady accumulation.

**When to apply** — As a research question, not a method: when a programme produces sudden, non-proportional changes (a breakthrough, a collapse in form, an injury), the authors' frame says to look for a change of state rather than a small linear effect. It supports the book's case for conjugate and delayed-effect thinking.

**When NOT to apply** — The page offers a research agenda ("may then be of profit"), no training study, so `untested`. Nothing here tells a coach what to programme. The authors call self-organisation by chance "One of the most controversial aspects" of the concept. Inference: borrowing terms from physics does not by itself explain an athlete's change; the claim needs data that the page does not give.

**Example** — The authors' own list of sudden "changes of state in adaptation space": "supercompensation, muscle injury or heart attacks" (PDF 486 / p.475).

**Related** — [[framework--four-types-of-stability-and-sudden-changes-of-fitness-state]], [[framework--butterfly-catastrophe-model-of-exercise-imbalance-injury-fig-8-9]] (Siff's catastrophe model, 8.8), [[framework--fuzzy-logic-model-of-energy-system-contribution-fig-8-10]]

# "Fuzzy Fitness": Physiological Thresholds Are Ranges, Not Points, and Athletes Control Performance by Feel

**What it is** — Under "Fuzzy Fitness" the authors argue that exercise science "still tends to be dominated by a type of thinking which was revered and promulgated by the ancient Grecians," in which "Everything belongs either to one category (set) or to another, but not to both concurrently" (PDF 486 / p.475, checked against the page image). Their list of fitness polarities: "aerobic vs anaerobic training, cardiovascular vs strength training, fit vs unfit, slow twitch vs fast twitch muscles, static vs dynamic, mobilisers vs stabilisers, and physical vs mental" (PDF 486 / p.475). Fuzzy logic, "a logical system based on the recognition that *everything is a matter of degree*," is the alternative: "no muscular activity is 100% aerobic or anaerobic. At any instant, the activity comprises a percentage of each" (PDF 487 / p.476, checked against the page image). In exercise physiology "it will caution us not to rigidly apply concepts such as 'lactate threshold' or any other threshold or turning 'point', for that matter, since this clearly implies that up to some level there is minimal lactate and a fraction above that level, there is suddenly abundant lactate," whereas "changes take place over a range which displays a relatively steep or relatively gradual slope" (PDF 487 / p.476).

**Why it works** — The authors' evidence is how athletes actually control effort: "an athlete competing in a distance event judges his pace by tuning into how hard or easy a given pace is ... He never operates in terms of absolute measures, precise calculations and percentage increases to ensure that his pulse rate is exactly 145 beats per minute"; "the athlete constantly uses vague concepts such as 'too fast', 'too low' or 'that feels good' to produce competitive excellence." So "sporting performance is far more typical of fuzzy, vague logic than it is of precise mathematical formulae," and fuzzy logic lets us "use apparently vague or inexact descriptions of processes to improve on the existing performance of systems which inappropriately use unwarranted precision in their controlling systems" (PDF 487 / p.476).

**When to apply** — Setting training zones from a lab threshold: treat the threshold as the middle of a band and let the athlete's perceived effort fine-tune within it. Designing programmes that mix qualities instead of assigning each session to one category. Eric's review: the baseline records that mRSI from daily CMJ testing was chosen "in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is 'objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were.'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74). Inference: that line is about a readiness marker, not about controlling effort within a session, so it does not conflict with the authors' point; the two answer different questions.

**When NOT to apply** — An argument from analogy and anecdote with no study, so `untested`. Read the either-or examples on PDF 487 with care: "Muscle hypertrophy is best developed by 8-12 repetitions of resistance training, strength by 3-5 repetitions, power by 1-3 repetitions" is the authors' example of rigid thinking they criticise, not a prescription. "Fuzzy logic, as discussed earlier" refers to earlier text this library has no entry for. The authors still accept that "Scientists can perform fairly accurate analysis under laboratory conditions"; the claim is about how precision is used, not against measurement.

**Example** — The authors' powerlifter: one "competing in the squat event has to judge when the depth of the squat is legally low enough to be passed, a feat which he achieves by purely subjective feeling based on experience" (PDF 487 / p.476).

**Related** — [[framework--fuzzy-logic-model-of-energy-system-contribution-fig-8-10]], [[claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]] (1.15), [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]] (training by perceived effort), [[framework--four-types-of-stability-and-sudden-changes-of-fitness-state]]
