# Fig 8.10: A Fuzzy-Logic Model Linking Exercise Intensity or Duration to the Blend of the Three Energy Systems

**What it is** — The authors give "An example of how fuzzy logic may be used to explain the relationship between the duration (or intensity) of activity at any moment to the contributions of the three main energy processes in the body (see 1.14)" (PDF 487 / p.476, checked against the page image). Fig 8.10, read from the page image (PDF 488 / p.477): the X axis is "EXERCISE INTENSITY," drawn as five overlapping fuzzy sets, Very low, Low, Medium, High, Very high, beside a vertical arrow "DURATION OF ACTIVITY" running from Long (top) to Brief (bottom). The Y axis is "RATE OF ENERGY PRODUCTION," drawn as three overlapping bell-shaped sets, Very Rapid, Intermediate, Slow, labelled underneath as HIGH ENERGY PHOSPHAGENS, NON-OXIDATIVE GLYCOLYTIC, OXIDATIVE GLYCOLYTIC. Three rules link them: "If X very low Then Y slow," "If X medium Then Y intermediate," "If X very high Then Y very rapid," each drawn as a fuzzy patch on a curve labelled "Y = F(X)." The caption: "The application of fuzzy logic to understanding the dependence of the intensity (or duration) of any exercise on the three major metabolic processes. The method uses rules that relate fuzzy sets of rates of energy production such as 'very rapid' to fuzzy sets of exercise duration such as 'very short'. The relationship between the X and Y sets produces a chain of fuzzy patches, which can approximate a performance curve Y = F(X)" (PDF 488 / p.477).

**Why it works** — The authors: "This model emphasizes that optimal efficiency for any given duration (or intensity) of exercise depends on the concurrent different contributions of the short, intermediate and long-term energy systems. This enables us to think less in terms of one activity being aerobic and another anaerobic, and to plan training so that the dynamic balance between the three energy mechanisms is shifted in the most appropriate direction for any given sport" (PDF 487 / p.476). The overlapping sets are the point: at any intensity more than one system contributes.

**When to apply** — Conditioning design for mixed-demand sports: describe each drill by where it sits on the intensity or duration axis and which blend it shifts toward, rather than labelling it "aerobic" or "anaerobic." Useful when teaching staff that energy systems overlap.

**When NOT to apply** — The figure is schematic: no times, intensities or percentage contributions are given, so it cannot be used to set work-rest ratios, and the entry is `untested`. The caption and figure do not match exactly: the caption speaks of duration sets "such as 'very short'," while the figure labels its sets by intensity (Very low to Very high) and marks duration only as an arrow from Long to Brief; no set is labelled "very short." Inference: the figure treats intensity and duration as the same axis run in opposite directions, which holds for maximal efforts but not for submaximal work that is both long and moderate. The text layer reads the curve label as "Y « F(X)"; the image shows "Y = F(X)."

**Example** — Rule three of the figure: "If X very high Then Y very rapid," with the Very Rapid set sitting over HIGH ENERGY PHOSPHAGENS (PDF 488 / p.477). Inference: a brief maximal sprint draws mostly on phosphagens, with the overlapping glycolytic set still contributing.

**Related** — [[claim--physiological-thresholds-are-ranges-and-athletes-regulate-performance-by-feel]], [[heuristic--field-sport-conditioning-favours-short-energy-systems-and-strength-before-endurance]] (8.2), [[claim--non-equilibrium-and-self-organisation-prigogine-as-a-model-for-performance-leaps]]

# Fig 8.10: A Fuzzy-Logic Model Linking Exercise Intensity or Duration to the Blend of the Three Energy Systems

**What it is** — The authors give "An example of how fuzzy logic may be used to explain the relationship between the duration (or intensity) of activity at any moment to the contributions of the three main energy processes in the body (see 1.14)" (PDF 487 / p.476, checked against the page image). Fig 8.10, read from the page image (PDF 488 / p.477): the X axis is "EXERCISE INTENSITY," drawn as five overlapping fuzzy sets, Very low, Low, Medium, High, Very high, beside a vertical arrow "DURATION OF ACTIVITY" running from Long (top) to Brief (bottom). The Y axis is "RATE OF ENERGY PRODUCTION," drawn as three overlapping bell-shaped sets, Very Rapid, Intermediate, Slow, labelled underneath as HIGH ENERGY PHOSPHAGENS, NON-OXIDATIVE GLYCOLYTIC, OXIDATIVE GLYCOLYTIC. Three rules link them: "If X very low Then Y slow," "If X medium Then Y intermediate," "If X very high Then Y very rapid," each drawn as a fuzzy patch on a curve labelled "Y = F(X)." The caption: "The application of fuzzy logic to understanding the dependence of the intensity (or duration) of any exercise on the three major metabolic processes. The method uses rules that relate fuzzy sets of rates of energy production such as 'very rapid' to fuzzy sets of exercise duration such as 'very short'. The relationship between the X and Y sets produces a chain of fuzzy patches, which can approximate a performance curve Y = F(X)" (PDF 488 / p.477).

**Why it works** — The authors: "This model emphasizes that optimal efficiency for any given duration (or intensity) of exercise depends on the concurrent different contributions of the short, intermediate and long-term energy systems. This enables us to think less in terms of one activity being aerobic and another anaerobic, and to plan training so that the dynamic balance between the three energy mechanisms is shifted in the most appropriate direction for any given sport" (PDF 487 / p.476). The overlapping sets are the point: at any intensity more than one system contributes.

**When to apply** — Conditioning design for mixed-demand sports: describe each drill by where it sits on the intensity or duration axis and which blend it shifts toward, rather than labelling it "aerobic" or "anaerobic." Useful when teaching staff that energy systems overlap.

**When NOT to apply** — The figure is schematic: no times, intensities or percentage contributions are given, so it cannot be used to set work-rest ratios, and the entry is `untested`. The caption and figure do not match exactly: the caption speaks of duration sets "such as 'very short'," while the figure labels its sets by intensity (Very low to Very high) and marks duration only as an arrow from Long to Brief; no set is labelled "very short." Inference: the figure treats intensity and duration as the same axis run in opposite directions, which holds for maximal efforts but not for submaximal work that is both long and moderate. The text layer reads the curve label as "Y « F(X)"; the image shows "Y = F(X)."

**Example** — Rule three of the figure: "If X very high Then Y very rapid," with the Very Rapid set sitting over HIGH ENERGY PHOSPHAGENS (PDF 488 / p.477). Inference: a brief maximal sprint draws mostly on phosphagens, with the overlapping glycolytic set still contributing.

# Russian Coaches' View: Most Nutritional Supplements Are Unwarranted Unless Periodised, and Chronic Use Can Lower the Training Effect

**What it is** — Under "Application of New Methods" the authors report the view of Russian coaches, not their own finding: "Russian coaches have already remarked on the indiscriminate use of nutritional ergogenic aids promoted widely by Western drug companies since drug testing became more rigorous. They consider that ingestion of most amino acid supplements, trace minerals and carbohydrate drinks is largely unwarranted and useless, especially since almost none of these supplements has been integrated into a carefully periodised training programme. They stress that the use of any *Biologically Active Substance* must be properly selected on the basis of a clear understanding of chrononutrition so that negative interactions and detrimental effects of prolonged usage can be avoided. They also point out that adaptation caused by chronic use of these substances can actually produce a lower training effect than would training without these supplements" (PDF 488-489 / pp.477-478, checked against the page images; italics in the original).

**Why it works** — The mechanism offered is accommodation, the same one the authors apply to all recovery and stimulation means: "regular reliance on any means to improve performance and to accelerate adaptation may be unwise because the system accommodates to them and they tend to lose their effectiveness" (PDF 488 / p.477). Inference: on this view a supplement taken every day becomes part of the baseline the body adapts around, so its acute effect fades and the adaptive stimulus it was masking may be lost.

**When to apply** — When an athlete takes several supplements daily with no link to the training phase: ask what each is for, when in the cycle it is needed, and whether it interacts with others. The authors' general rule for all such modalities: they "should not be applied in isolation, but integrated correctly into the overall training programme" (PDF 488 / p.477).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a reported coaching opinion with no study, so `untested`. Inference: carbohydrate intake in particular has a large evidence base since the book was written; do not use this page to argue against fuelling. Supplement education at Baylor sits with Performance Nutrition, a separate unit (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 159, paraphrased); route any change in an athlete's supplements through that unit rather than through this entry. "Chrononutrition" is named but not defined on the page.

**Example** — The three categories the Russian coaches call "largely unwarranted and useless": "most amino acid supplements, trace minerals and carbohydrate drinks" (PDF 488 / p.477).

**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]] (6.9.3), [[heuristic--rotate-restorative-means-and-rest-local-procedures]] (8.6: accommodation to restorative means), [[heuristic--keep-all-staff-in-contact-and-use-massage-specialists-as-early-overtraining-detectors]]

# Keep Everyone Who Works With an Athlete in Regular Contact, and Treat the Massage Therapist's Hands as an Early Overtraining Detector

**What it is** — In "Application of New Methods" the authors report that, because constant use of the same massage "can diminish its benefits or even inhibit performance," "Russian coaches recommend *partial restoration* and *limited zone massage*, at the same time communicating regularly with the massage specialists who work with their athletes. These specialists can usually manually detect in the soft tissues of athletes that may be of great relevance in the early diagnosis of overtraining or unbalanced training" (PDF 488 / p.477, checked against the page image; the sentence is printed with a word missing after "detect"). The general rule: "An important implication of this is that it is essential for all personnel working with an athlete in any way whatsoever to keep in regular contact to ensure that all training programmes are properly monitored and modified, if necessary" (PDF 488 / p.477). They add that "all Russian coaches and physical education coaches spend 700-900 hours over several semesters learning and practising sports massage."

**Why it works** — The therapist's hands sample the tissue several times a week, so changes in tone or tenderness can show before performance drops. The kinaesthetic section later describes the same practice: "massage specialists used their hands to palpate the muscles and other soft tissues to identify patterns of tension and development in the bodies of their athletes," and "The results were communicated to coaches" (PDF 489-490 / pp.478-479).

**When to apply** — Build a short, regular channel between soft-tissue staff and the strength and sport coaches (a weekly note on tone, tenderness or asymmetry per athlete). Use it as one input to load decisions, alongside objective tests. Eric's review: "The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 48; the line continues past a dash that no single discipline owns the athlete's development). Inference: the authors' "all personnel ... keep in regular contact" is that wheel put into practice.

**When NOT to apply** — No validation of palpation as an overtraining marker is given, so `untested`. The printed sentence about what specialists detect is incomplete (a missing object after "detect"), so the exact finding is unclear. The 700-900 hours figure describes Russian coach education and is not a target. Palpation findings are a prompt for a closer look, not a diagnosis.

**Example** — The authors' pairing: partial restoration and limited zone massage, plus regular talk with the massage specialist, who may detect early signs of "overtraining or unbalanced training" (PDF 488 / p.477).

**Related** — [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]] (palpation soreness as a marker), [[heuristic--rotate-restorative-means-and-rest-local-procedures]], [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]], [[principle--pair-objective-and-subjective-tests-because-rpe-can-miss-a-poor-functional-state]], [[heuristic--use-touch-and-kinaesthetic-cues-to-teach-positions-and-detect-tension]]

Their main example: "invasive testing of metabolic changes is replaced or supplemented by use of *seismotonography*, a system which uses mechanical means to measure muscle tension (stiffness) and damping ratio (Siff, 1986). These measures can be very informative, because changes in muscle tone during and after training can give an indication of whether the training is sufficient or excessive, if different restoration means are optimally effective and if the athlete has recovered enough to resume training" (PDF 489 / p.478). With electromyography and plethysmography it is "especially applied to assess the presence of excessive hypertrophy," and "Estimation of the strength deficit of contractile and non-contractile tissue forms part of this analysis to ascertain whether the training should focus on promoting hypertrophic or nervous changes in the body (see Ch 1)" (PDF 489 / p.478). # Use Touch and Other Kinaesthetic Cues to Teach Positions, and Vary Them So Athletes Do Not Habituate

**What it is** — Under "Kinaesthetic Manipulation and Education" the authors call the kinaesthetic sense the real sixth sense: "the sense of being aware of where the body and its components are in space in time," built on proprioceptors integrated "with the senses of balance and touch, as well as with subtle control mechanisms involving breathing." "Any contact with external objects such sporting apparatus, an opponent, clothing and shoes, can, via their effect on the kinaesthetic sense, profoundly influence performance" (PDF 489 / p.478, checked against the page image). In Russia and Eastern Europe "touch, massage, visual cueing, the sketching of movements and other kinaesthetic awareness activities were not only useful in therapy, but also to enhance coaching skills and athletic performance." Coaches learned to "touch, stroke or strongly press the appropriate areas of their athletes to relax, stimulate, delay fatigue or guide them during training," and "how to touch or hold parts of the body to facilitate learning of movements, improve 'visualisation' (mental mapping) of movement patterns and characteristics, and to increase strength of specific stabilisers or mobilisers" (PDF 489-490 / pp.478-479, checked against the page images). The caution that came with it: "to avoid overusing the same kinaesthetic strategies ... to ensure that athletes do not habituate to the same mode of learning, recovery or control" (PDF 490 / p.479).

**Why it works** — The authors' account is that force control "relies on kinaesthetic awareness of what is happening within the musculoskeletal system," and touch adds a direct signal about which part to move or tense (PDF 490 / p.479). Inference: a hand on the back or hip gives a lifter a location for the cue that words alone may not.

**When to apply** — Teaching novices start and pull positions: "touching of the back, head and buttocks was used to teach novices the starting and pulling positions in the Olympic lifts, as well as many manoeuvres in gymnastics, dance, track-and-field and swimming" (PDF 490 / p.479). Rotate the cue type over weeks. Eric's review: "Constraints-led and external-cue coaching are not part of Eric's practice. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q25): 'I don't apply it, as I don't fully understand it. I want to know more.'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 170). Inference: a touch cue directs attention to the body, so it is not the external-cue method the baseline names; it is a separate option the baseline does not address.

**When NOT to apply** — The page reports practice and cites Russian periodicals (*Legkaya Atletika*, *Tyezhelaya Atletika*, *Teoriya i Praktika*), not studies, so `untested`. Inference: hands-on cueing needs the athlete's consent and a clear explanation of where and why, especially in mixed-sex coaching; the page does not discuss this. The pressure-point, neurolymphatic and acupressure techniques the author was taught "between 1992-1994 by a member of the Bulgarian national weightlifting team" (PDF 490 / p.479) are reported, not evaluated. The same paragraph says Bulgarian coaches and PE students spent "three semesters" on restoration and massage; that is context, not a target. The page cross-references the shoe and belt material to "(8.8)" and "(Ch 8.8)" (PDF 489 / p.478); both are in 8.9 in this edition.

**Example** — The book's own reflex example of an unwanted kinaesthetic effect: "forward flexion of the neck during a squat, clean or deadlift can cause a reflex relaxation of the spine, disrupt the optimal lifting pattern and endanger the lifter" (PDF 489 / p.478).

**Related** — [[framework--kinaesthetic-system-and-feedforward-visualization]] (1.14), [[heuristic--blindfolded-training-enhances-proprioceptive-skill-acquisition]], [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]] (neck flexion and spinal reflexes), [[claim--lifting-belt-cues-back-position-by-proprioception-but-does-not-keep-the-back-flat]], [[case-study--farfel-elite-weightlifters-misjudge-exerted-force-by-up-to-100-percent]], [[heuristic--keep-all-staff-in-contact-and-use-massage-specialists-as-early-overtraining-detectors]]

# Farfel et al (1975): Even Elite Weightlifters Misjudged the Force They Were Exerting, With Errors of Up to 100% Common

**What it is** — The authors introduce it with a principle (in italics on the page): "*The production and control of muscular force is one of the primary tasks in all sport*, a process which relies on kinaesthetic awareness of what is happening within the musculoskeletal system in response to events in the sporting environment" (PDF 490 / p.479, checked against the page image). Then the study: "Farfel et al (1975) set out to ascertain the type of information upon which this motor control is based by examining the ability of weightlifters to estimate the forces which they exert during different lifts and different stages of various lifts (Sokolov, 1982). After studying a group of elite Russian weightlifters (Masters of Sport Class), they concluded that the ability of even world class weightlifters to estimate the force (relative to their experience of what a 1RM load feels like) they are exerting at different stages of the Olympic lifts under static and explosive conditions is very poor. Measurements made on special pulling dynamometers showed that errors of as much as 100% were common" (PDF 490 / p.479).

**Why it works** — The study's own explanation: "It was concluded that this weakness in being able to accurately control force is the result of inappropriate training methods and that the lifters needed to systematically perfect their 'muscle sense', both by developing an acute inner feel for kinaesthetic processes and by using biofeedback information from specialised dynamometers to enable them to quantitatively imprint this awareness" (PDF 490 / p.479).

**When to apply** — When a programme relies on an athlete's sense of effort to set or adjust load: this result says even elite lifters' estimates of force can be badly off. Use measured feedback (bar velocity, force plate or dynamometer readouts) to calibrate the feel, as the study recommends. Eric's review: the baseline chose mRSI from daily CMJ testing because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74). Inference: Farfel's result is a parallel case for measured over felt indicators, though Farfel tested force estimation within lifts, not daily readiness.

**When NOT to apply** — The population (elite Masters of Sport) and instrument (special pulling dynamometers) are named, and the conditions (static and explosive, different lift stages, relative to 1RM feel) are stated, so `supported` under the standard the 8c review applied to partly described Vorobyev data; but no n, no error distribution and no protocol are given, and the study is reported second-hand through Sokolov (1982). "As much as 100%" is an upper figure described as "common," not a mean. The cause ("inappropriate training methods") is the study authors' conclusion, not tested. Inference: this does not contradict RPE-based training; it says the felt scale needs calibrating, which is what the authors propose.

**Example** — Elite Russian weightlifters, asked to estimate their force at different stages of the Olympic lifts against their sense of a 1RM, made errors "of as much as 100%" on special pulling dynamometers (PDF 490 / p.479).

# Teaching a Skill in Reverse Order, or in Components, Beat Natural-Sequence Teaching: the Snatch Learned From the Drop Backwards Was 40 Percent More Effective

**What it is** — Under "Advances in Methods of Coaching" the authors write: "Sometimes, apparently logical methods of learning are not necessarily found to be the most effective. For instance, Russian researchers have discovered that teaching a new movement in its natural sequential order from start to finish is not necessarily as effective as *teaching the action in the reverse order* (Vorobyev, 1978). They found that learning of the Olympic weightlifting snatch from the final drop phase backwards to the starting pull is 40 percent more effective than the conventional order of learning. They also examined the effect of breaking sporting movements down into basic components and having athletes learn each element separately before attempting the whole movement. This method of *component learning* also proved to be superior to the conventional method of natural sequence learning" (PDF 490-491 / pp.479-480, checked against the page images; italics in the original).

**Why it works** — The page gives no mechanism. The authors frame it under motor learning: "An understanding of how to programme the human biocomputer effectively by sensory and motor activity is vital to the growth of performance," given that "structure and function in the central nervous system is not as rigidly determined as hitherto thought (Ch 1: under 'Neural Changes with Training')" (PDF 490 / p.479). Inference: starting from the receiving position means every later practice of the earlier phases ends in a position already learned, so the lifter always finishes in a familiar place.

**When to apply** — Teaching the snatch (and likely the clean and jerk) to novices: begin with the overhead squat and receiving position, then add the drop, then the pull, ending with the full lift from the floor. Use component practice where a whole skill is too complex to learn at once. Eric's review: the baseline's operating value includes "teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 41). Inference: reverse-order teaching is one way to order those basic positions within a lift.

**When NOT to apply** — "40 percent more effective" has no stated measure (speed of learning, technique rating, load lifted), no sample and no follow-up on the page; Vorobyev (1978) is cited, not described, so `untested`. The component-learning result has no number at all. Inference: the result is for a closed skill with a fixed end position; open, reactive skills may not break down the same way.

**Example** — The authors' snatch case: learning "from the final drop phase backwards to the starting pull" was "40 percent more effective than the conventional order of learning" (PDF 490 / p.479).

# Technology Changes the Athlete's Environment; Coaching Methods Change the Athlete, So Technology Must Come With Better Pedagogy

**What it is** — The authors open "Advances in Methods of Coaching" with: "Sometimes the current focus on physiological and biomechanical measurement in sports science makes one lose sight of the importance of improving our methods of motor learning" (PDF 490 / p.479, checked against the page image). They close it by gathering the book's methods: "When this is considered along with other advances in training such as reverse order learning, cognitive plyometrics, periodisation guided by ratings of perceived effort, biofeedback learning, and conjugate sequence loading, it becomes apparent that technology must always be accompanied by progress in coaching methodology and pedagogy. Methods derived from teaching intellectual subjects (such as suggestology and autogenics) can also prove to be valuable in accelerating and perfecting the learning of sporting skills (Ostrander & Schroder, 1979, 1994; Hutchison, 1986). In this context, it should be noted that technology changes the external environment of the athlete, whereas coaching methods (sometimes via the use of technology) change the athlete" (PDF 491 / p.480, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — A device that measures or loads the athlete only alters what the athlete meets; adaptation and skill come from how the coach uses that information to teach. Inference: the parenthesis "(sometimes via the use of technology)" is the key: technology earns its place when it feeds a coaching method, such as biofeedback or RPE-guided periodisation, both on the authors' list.

**When to apply** — Before buying or adopting a monitoring device: name the coaching decision or teaching method it will change. When reviewing a sport-science service: check that its outputs reach the coach in a form that changes what the athlete does.

18	**Why it works** — The page gives no mechanism. The authors frame it under motor learning: "An understanding of how to programme the human biocomputer effectively by sensory and motor activity is vital to the growth of performance," given that "structure and function in the central nervous system is not as rigidly determined as hitherto thought (Ch 1: under 'Neural Changes with Training')" (PDF 490 / p.479). Inference: starting from the receiving position means every later practice of the earlier phases ends in a position already learned, so the lifter always finishes in a familiar place.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Teaching the snatch (and likely the clean and jerk) to novices: begin with the overhead squat and receiving position, then add the drop, then the pull, ending with the full lift from the floor. Use component practice where a whole skill is too complex to learn at once. Eric's review: the baseline's operating value includes "teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 41). Inference: reverse-order teaching is one way to order those basic positions within a lift.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — "40 percent more effective" has no stated measure (speed of learning, technique rating, load lifted), no sample and no follow-up on the page; Vorobyev (1978) is cited, not described, so `untested`. The component-learning result has no number at all. Inference: the result is for a closed skill with a fixed end position; open, reactive skills may not break down the same way.
23	
24	**Example** — The authors' snatch case: learning "from the final drop phase backwards to the starting pull" was "40 percent more effective than the conventional order of learning" (PDF 490 / p.479).
25	
26	**Related** — [[principle--technology-changes-the-environment-coaching-methods-change-the-athlete]], [[heuristic--use-touch-and-kinaesthetic-cues-to-teach-positions-and-detect-tension]]

18	**Why it works** — The therapist's hands sample the tissue several times a week, so changes in tone or tenderness can show before performance drops. The kinaesthetic section later describes the same practice: "massage specialists used their hands to palpate the muscles and other soft tissues to identify patterns of tension and development in the bodies of their athletes," and "The results were communicated to coaches" (PDF 489-490 / pp.478-479).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Build a short, regular channel between soft-tissue staff and the strength and sport coaches (a weekly note on tone, tenderness or asymmetry per athlete). Use it as one input to load decisions, alongside objective tests. Eric's review: "The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 48; the line continues past a dash that no single discipline owns the athlete's development). Inference: the authors' "all personnel ... keep in regular contact" is that wheel put into practice.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — No validation of palpation as an overtraining marker is given, so `untested`. The printed sentence about what specialists detect is incomplete (a missing object after "detect"), so the exact finding is unclear. The 700-900 hours figure describes Russian coach education and is not a target. Palpation findings are a prompt for a closer look, not a diagnosis.
23

18	**Why it works** — Because protection depends on so many qualities and on the state the joint is in when the load arrives, no single quality can be trained to cover it. The authors draw that conclusion: "General strength training on its own is inadequate to guarantee improved muscular protection for the body. The large range of processes implicated in musculoskeletal protection emphasizes the importance of special strength training in the properly-sequenced, multi-faceted manner discussed earlier in this book" (PDF 483 / p.472).
19	
20	**When to apply** — As a checklist when a programme's stated aim is injury resilience: count which of the listed qualities it trains (starting strength, reactive ability, eccentric strength and endurance, isometric strength after movement stops, strength-flexibility, connective tissue) and in which initial states (moving, holding, at rest). Inference: the "part completely at rest" case argues for some training where load arrives unexpectedly on a relaxed or holding limb, not only on a muscle already braced.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — The list is the authors' synthesis with no study attached, so `untested`. It names qualities, not tests or doses. It is about protection under imposed load and does not rank the factors. "Overflow or compensatory muscle activity" is the same irradiation idea the book uses elsewhere; it is not separately evidenced here.
23	
24	**Example** — Inference: a defensive back hit while planting (eccentric state) needs eccentric strength and reactive recruitment; the same player hit while standing still needs isometric strength and quick onset. The authors' list covers both through "initial conditions at the moment of loading" (PDF 483 / p.472).
25	
26	**Related** — [[claim--strong-muscles-protect-joints-only-when-contracted-in-the-right-pattern]], [[claim--ligaments-carry-more-load-than-muscles-under-joint-traction-basmajian]], [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]]

18	**Why it works** — Protection is an act, not a property: the muscle has to be on, in the right pattern, at the moment of loading. If reflexes are slow or absent near end range, size cannot help; the ligaments take the load instead. The factors that decide whether protection happens are in [[framework--factors-that-determine-muscular-protection-of-a-joint]].
19	
20	**When to apply** — In contact sports, when hypertrophy or maximal strength is sold as neck or spine injury protection. Inference: in American football, add work that trains the timing and pattern of contraction under unexpected or end-range loads (reactive and eccentric work, braced positions) alongside general strength, since the authors say general strength alone does not guarantee protection.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — The EMG studies are not cited on this page, so `untested`. The claim does not say strength is useless for protection; the authors call general strength "inadequate to guarantee" it, and the next paragraph lists eccentric, isometric and connective-tissue strength among the factors that decide it. It is a claim about joints under imposed load, not about performance.
23	
24	**Example** — The authors' contrast: "A relaxed massive and powerful muscle is almost as useless as a relaxed small muscle in protecting a joint" (PDF 483 / p.472), aimed at contact-sport texts that say large muscles prevent spinal injury.
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--factors-that-determine-muscular-protection-of-a-joint]], [[claim--ligaments-carry-more-load-than-muscles-under-joint-traction-basmajian]]

18	**Why it works** — Two mechanisms on the page: a soft sole delays the force reaching the foot, so the reflex that extends and stabilises the leg fires later; and because where pressure lands on the sole sets the limb's extension (Guyton, 1984), a shoe that moves that pressure point changes muscle recruitment. Inference: the second point is about shoe shape, so it applies to firm shoes with an unusual geometry as well as to cushioned ones.
19	
20	**When to apply** — When an athlete's landing or cutting control looks slow or unstable in a very cushioned shoe; when a new shoe with a different heel or sole profile coincides with a change in movement pattern. The authors' general remedy is to choose shoes "appropriate for the individual and the sport" and use them "safely and correctly, if necessary by studying slow motion replays of the action involved" (PDF 480 / p.469).
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — No timing data are given for the delay, and only Guyton (1984), a physiology text, is cited, so `untested`. The page does not say how much delay matters for injury. This is the same reflex the book cites in 5.2.4 to argue against very soft plyometric footwear and floors, so it is one argument repeated, not two independent findings.
23	
24	**Example** — The authors' fitness-class contrast: bare feet on firm high-density mats preserve "proprioceptive efficiency" and avoid the longer heel-to-ankle lever arm a shoe adds (PDF 480 / p.469).
25	
26	**Related** — [[heuristic--plyometric-surface-footwear-and-simple-apparatus]] (5.2.4: soft footwear delays "the triggering of the positive supportive reaction of the foot"), [[heuristic--do-some-daily-barefoot-locomotion-to-keep-the-plantar-protective-reflex]], [[claim--cushioned-athletic-shoes-have-not-been-shown-to-prevent-lower-limb-injury]]

18	**Why it works** — In a free standing movement the load is shared and redistributed across a chain of joints; fix one link and the neighbouring joint takes what it would have shed. The seated-back-extension bullet gives the same reasoning for the spine: "the seated position does not allow the hip and knee joints any freedom to modify the magnitude or direction of loading on the lower back," so it "can impose a greater compressive and transverse loading on lower spinal structures than an equivalent deadlift" (PDF 481 / p.470).
19	
20	**When to apply** — Before choosing a machine exercise, ask which joints it fixes and which joint sits next to them; that neighbour is where the extra stress goes. Two remedies from the page: switch to the free-weight equivalent, or control speed and "transition accelerations." Useful when an athlete reports knee pain on leg extensions or back pain on seated presses.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — The authors say "usually," not always, and give no measurements, so `untested`. Inference: in rehabilitation, fixing a joint on purpose to protect it or to isolate a weak muscle can be the right call; the principle says where the cost lands, not that the cost is never worth paying. The 4.2.7 entry already gives the leg-extension knee-shear example with its reasoning ([[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]]); this entry is the general rule the 8.10 list states.
23	
24	**Example** — The authors' own: the seated leg extension "tends to immobilise the hip joint, so that greater stress falls on the nearby knee joint" (PDF 483 / p.472).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--machine-safety-checklist-hazards-and-countermeasures]], [[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]] (4.2.7: seated knee extension and knee shear)

18	**Why it works** — Anchoring the feet lets the hip flexors pull the trunk up before the abdominals have curled it, which the authors link to spinal stress. Repeated short-range hip flexion in volume, in their account, shortens the hip's range, which then costs running, jumping and kicking. Inference: the loaded lunge stretch restores hip extension range in the same muscle the sit-ups shortened.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Programmes that use anchored sit-ups or sit-up boards in volume, especially for runners, jumpers, kickers and weightlifters (the page names jerking). Cue the curl-up before hip flexion, keep it slow, and finish with long, deep upright lunges.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Not a ban on hip-flexor work: the bullet just before says "the abdominal and hip flexor muscles are meant to function in an integrated fashion, so there is nothing intrinsically 'wrong' about doing abdominal exercises which also recruit the iliopsoas group; what may be most risky is the inappropriate timing of the involvement of the different muscles in any trunk exercises" (PDF 481-482 / pp.470-471). The range-loss claim has no data on the page, so `untested`. The page does not give a stretch dose.
23	
24	**Example** — The authors' remedy: "Long, deep lunges with the trunk upright" after limited-range sit-ups (PDF 482 / p.471).

20	**When to apply** — Programmes that use anchored sit-ups or sit-up boards in volume, especially for runners, jumpers, kickers and weightlifters (the page names jerking). Cue the curl-up before hip flexion, keep it slow, and finish with long, deep upright lunges.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Not a ban on hip-flexor work: the bullet just before says "the abdominal and hip flexor muscles are meant to function in an integrated fashion, so there is nothing intrinsically 'wrong' about doing abdominal exercises which also recruit the iliopsoas group; what may be most risky is the inappropriate timing of the involvement of the different muscles in any trunk exercises" (PDF 481-482 / pp.470-471). The range-loss claim has no data on the page, so `untested`. The page does not give a stretch dose.
23	
24	**Example** — The authors' remedy: "Long, deep lunges with the trunk upright" after limited-range sit-ups (PDF 482 / p.471).
25	
26	**Related** — [[framework--machine-safety-checklist-hazards-and-countermeasures]], [[claim--trunk-rotation-is-driven-by-the-obliques-not-the-erector-spinae]] (7.4.2: sit-up variants shift work between rectus abdominis, obliques and psoas)

"framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique": "From 8.12: [[claim--physiological-thresholds-are-ranges-and-athletes-regulate-performance-by-feel]] (athletes control effort by feel), [[case-study--farfel-elite-weightlifters-misjudge-exerted-force-by-up-to-100-percent]] (felt force needs calibrating), [[principle--technology-changes-the-environment-coaching-methods-change-the-athlete]] (RPE-guided periodisation listed as a coaching advance).",

"heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation": "From 8.12: [[claim--most-nutritional-supplements-are-unwarranted-unless-periodised-russian-coaches]] (Russian coaches: chronic supplement use can lower the training effect).",

}
ALSO = {
"principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting": "**Also in 8.9** — 8.9.1 repeats the rule and points back here: \"While it is advisable during many exercises to inhale before the effort and exhale with the effort, without holding the breath, it is important to hold the breath briefly while raising any load in the standing position. As discussed earlier (3.4.9), this is essential because the breath-holding (or Valsalva) manoeuvre increases the pressure in your abdomen and supports your lower spine.\" It adds the time limit: \"Prolonged breath-holding (of more than a few seconds) causes dramatic increase in blood-pressure, followed by sudden drop in this pressure after exhalation, so it is definitely not advisable for anyone, particularly older folk and those with cardiovascular disease\" (PDF 478 / p.467, checked against the page image). The 75 percent lung-volume figure (Vorobyev, 1978) recurs on PDF 479 / p.468. See [[claim--lifting-belt-restrains-abdominal-pressure-and-supports-the-stomach-more-than-the-back]] (the belt as external restraint for the held-breath pressure), [[claim--lifting-belt-cues-back-position-by-proprioception-but-does-not-keep-the-back-flat]], [[claim--rectus-abdominis-barely-contracts-in-lifting-so-train-obliques-with-side-bending-and-twisting]].",
"heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use": "**Also in 8.10** — Section 8.10 calls the belief that machines are \"intrinsically safer than free weights and require far less skill\" a \"fallacy\" and ends: \"continuous observation and spotting are just as important for machines as for free weights exercises if the safety claims of machine manufacturers are to be realised in practice\" (PDF 480 and 483 / pp.469 and 472, checked against the page images). See [[framework--machine-safety-checklist-hazards-and-countermeasures]] (the 24-point list) and [[principle--a-machine-that-immobilises-one-joint-shifts-stress-to-adjacent-joints]].",
"claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals": "**Also in 8.10** — A safety argument for the same preference: machine circuits that \"compel you to race against timing devices\" make it \"far more likely that you will not take the time to correctly stabilise your body, use correct technique or avoid reliance on momentum,\" so \"Interval Circuit Training (ICT) with carefully controlled, slower use of heavier loads and rest periods between stations tends to be safer than hastily executed, lower intensity Continuous Circuit Training (CCT)\" (PDF 482 / p.471, checked against the page image). See [[framework--machine-safety-checklist-hazards-and-countermeasures]].",
"heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts": "**Also in 8.12** — The kinaesthetic section repeats it: \"forward flexion of the neck during a squat, clean or deadlift can cause a reflex relaxation of the spine, disrupt the optimal lifting pattern and endanger the lifter\" (PDF 489 / p.478, checked against the page image). See [[heuristic--use-touch-and-kinaesthetic-cues-to-teach-positions-and-detect-tension]].",
"heuristic--loadless-training-broomstick-protocol": "**Also in 8.12** — Under \"Non-Physical Factors\": \"Other research in which athletes performed loadless weightlifting movements with a broomstick while imagining effort against maximal loads revealed improvements in strength and skill (Kovalik, 1978)\" (PDF 484 / p.473, checked against the page image). See [[claim--mental-state-and-goal-specific-visualisation-raise-strength-and-speed]].",
"claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect": "**Also in 8.12** — The same faith-factor point, applied to mind-body courses: their success, \"however outrageous and unscientific their methodologies may be, has a great deal to do with the placebo effect (or faith factor).
